newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian stock market sees new inflows, optimism.
newsitem.headline: Russian stock market sees new inflows, optimism.

text.p: New investment money is flowing into Russia, where runaway yields on stocks are falling but market stability is increasing, analysts and traders said on Tuesday.
"The flows are coming from constantly increasing weighting from Western portfolio investors who already know the market," United City Bank research director Christopher Granville said.
Russia's generally hot stock market is setting new records in its feverish climb.

The Russian Trading System 22-share index opened at a record 369.15 on Tuesday after closing at a record 369.00 on Monday. It began the year below 200 and saw most of its appreciation in the first two months of the year.
Traders say a few major orders by conservative investors have injected a sense of optimism into the market, which has zigzagged over the last six weeks.
"It feels like the start of a trend," said Brunswick Director Martin Diggle.
"There are more serious, longer-term investors," he added, comparing the situation now to earlier market records, which investors later branded as false starts.
Some traders said there were more allocations by new investors than seasoned ones, though the spurt of funds was too new to characterise easily.
Conservative mainstream emerging market investors are increasingly seen as the driving force in Russia, which until recently was the territory of high-risk hedge funds.
Wall Street has hit its own new highs as worries about risks closer to home have eased -- which has allowed some investors to focus now on Russia.
Yields on the Russian Treasury-bill market have plummeted since early May, testing average yields below 20 percent in rouble terms. They were around 200 percent a year ago.
But foreign flows have been steady and could jump if yields on GKO discount Treasury bills rise a couple of points, Renaissance Capital research director Dirk Damrau said.

He said $500 million to $1 billion could flow into Russian domestic government securities over the next six weeks if yields rise that much. Market turnover is up to about $1 billion daily and the T-bill market as a whole is about $50 billion.
"GKOs have become a mainstream instrument for emerging market investors," he said.
"Even at the lower level of yields, Russia still offers relative value. There have been no wholesale departures despite yields 1,000 basis points less than six weeks ago."

As Russian markets become more mainstream, foreign investor classes are becoming more defined and the few investors likely to move between T-bills and equities, such as hedge funds, have left the market, analysts say.
Russian capital is more flexible but Damrau said only the foreign exchange and GKO markets offered significant liquidity.
Corporations have begun buying T-bills, he said, instead of moving money into dollars, which helped the central bank boost foreign currency reserves by 30 percent in May. They doubled in April.
"The big decision is to hold in cash roubles rather than dollars," Damrau said. "Corporates are buying GKOs."

Russian banks have also been moving into equities but not with sufficient force to sustain a boom, as the banks must still maintain high liquidity and reasonable stability -- both of which Russia's stock market is less able to provide.
